zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical reference consulted: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, supplied page subset. Source: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; licensed CC BY 4.0: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . Diplomatic readings are based on the supplied BnF scan; corrections and English review notes are this reviewer’s work, not a transcription supplied by NINJAL.

runs.text: A intereiza do gouerno he virtude, & boa

lines.note: Continues the meicun example from f313: integrity in government is a virtue or good quality of the ruler. The scan separates A from intereiza; the unusual printed intereiza sequence is retained rather than silently regularized to inteireza.

runs.text: parte do bom ſenhor, ou Rey.

lines.note: Completes the reference to the good lord or king. This is the translation of the preceding page’s Japanese sentence, not a new headword.
Meidei is paraphrased as sake ni yoo and glossed as getting drunk or drinking excessively. The independent headword begins flush with the other entries, so its provisional indentation is removed.
Ber completes beber, excessive drinking of wine in the Portuguese. The source’s vinho is not replaced with the Japanese beverage name.

runs.text: Meido. Curaqi michi. i, Xixite yuqu mi-

lines.note: Meido, explained as a dark path and the path taken after death, begins a new flush-left entry. Mi- is the first part of michi on the following physical row.

runs.text: Caminho por onde hum vai depois de

lines.note: Chi completes michi, followed by the path one takes after death. This mixed Japanese-and-Portuguese continuation remains indented.
Completes “after death” and introduces meido ni omomuku. Cami- starts caminhar; the printed vomomuqu retains historical initial vo-.

runs.text: nhar na outra vida pera o inferno, ou outro

lines.note: Nhar completes caminhar, proceeding in the other life toward hell or another place. This reflects the source’s religious explanation, not an added doctrinal claim.
Lugar completes the alternative destination. The short continuation is kept as its own physical row.
Meidô is paraphrased as nari ugoku and glossed as the earth moving or trembling. The circumflex distinguishes this printed form from Meido above; the headword is flush-left.
The example shihoo ni meidô su describes shaking in every direction. The scan retains a caron in Xifǒni and a circumflex in meidô, not one uniform long-vowel sign.
Completes the translation about the earth trembling everywhere. Aterra is preserved as supplied, while the clearly upright S. is separated from Portuguese italics.
Meifacu means clarity and starts its own flush-left entry. It is followed by the adjectival form meifacuna, rather than being a continuation of the earthquake example.
Meifacuna describes something clear, such as an argument or reason. The nasal mark in razão is preserved.
Meifit names excellent writing or painting. The paragraph sign and abbreviated Itẽ then begin a related sense referring to the maker.
The related sense is an eminent writer or painter. The source’s eſcriuão and inſigne are retained in historical spelling.

runs.text: Receita de mezinhas pera algũa in-

lines.note: Meifô is a medicinal recipe for an illness. The circumflex in the headword and the line-end in- are both visible.
Firmidade completes infirmidade across the physical break. No modern e is introduced to change it to enfermidade.
Meigan is paraphrased as akirakana manako, clear eyes. The direct eye sense precedes the metaphorical person-of-learning sense.
Item adds a person of great knowledge as another sense of meigan. This is an indented supplementary gloss, not a separately printed Japanese headword.
Meigo contrasts mayoi and satoru, erring and understanding or finding the right way. The Portuguese Errar and acertar express the same opposition.
Meigo wa ware ni ari puts error and understanding in oneself. The scan separates & a and shows no hyphen after the isolated a that continues as acertar below.
Certar completes acertar; the gloss says these lie in oneself. The visible word separation em mim is restored, and the entire upright Bup. is treated as the Buddhist usage label.
The homonymous meigo means niece while honoring the person concerned. The source’s peßoa retains the printed ligature-like double-s sort.
Meiguẽ denotes good or excellent words. The nasal abbreviation is over e, and the Japanese reading is meigen, not a literal gu-e sequence from the automatic hint.
Meigen wo yuu, alternatively haku, illustrates saying excellent words. The caron on yǔ and the separate alternative marker l, are preserved.
Completes the good-and-excellent-words gloss. This is the Portuguese continuation of the two Japanese verb alternatives.

runs.text: Meiguet. Aqiracana tçuqi. l, na aru tçuqi.

lines.note: Meiguet is paraphrased as a clear or renowned moon. The historical clipped final t in the headword is preserved, rather than expanded to modern -getsu.

runs.text: Lũa clara, & nomeada que he aos 15. dias

lines.note: The celebrated clear moon is specified as occurring on the fifteenth day. The scan plainly prints 15., correcting the OCR’s Es.; Lũa keeps its nasal mark.
Completes the date with the eighth month. This date belongs to the historical source’s calendrical description; it is not converted to a modern Gregorian date.
Meiguiocu is paraphrased as na aru tama, a renowned precious stone. The visible separation Na aru is restored; no- continues nomeada below.
Meada completes the renowned-stone definition. The final upright S. marks written usage and is kept outside the italic gloss.

runs.text: Mei-i. Na aru cuſuxi. i, Meijinno cuſuxi.

lines.note: Mei-i means an eminent physician, paraphrased with na aru kusushi and meijin no kusushi. The internal hyphen in Mei-i is printed and is not a physical line-break sign.
The Portuguese confirms an eminent physician. This gloss keeps inſigne rather than a modern orthographic replacement.
Meiji, meizuru, meijita concerns penetrating inward. The following example applies the expression to words reaching the heart.
Onkotoba mo kimo ni meijita says that the words penetrated deeply. The upright Feiq. is a citation label; its terminal period is also roman and the whole label is marked for typeface review.

runs.text: Lib. 1. As ſuas palauras penetrarão lhe o

lines.note: Lib. 1. belongs to the italic citation apparatus, followed by the translation of the words penetrating the person’s heart. The historical penetrarão spelling is retained.
Coração completes the translation. Its physical indentation is restored instead of leaving this Portuguese continuation flush with new headwords.
Meijin is a person eminent in some art or quality, paraphrased as na no aru hito. The line-end al- begins the following algũa.
Gũa completes algũa in the reference to an art or quality. The scan shows this as an indented continuation, not a new entry.
Meijǒ is an excellent or renowned fortress. The caron over the last vowel is visible and retained.
Mejiro names a small bird without a species description in the Portuguese. The diplomatic spelling Mejiro is retained, not normalized to a modern transliteration.
Meimei means each person individually. Meimei ni oku- begins the example of giving or sending something to each.

runs.text: Dar, ou mandar a cada hum

lines.note: Ri completes okuri before tamauaru. The scan has a comma after tamauaru, not a period, and the entire line is an indented example continuation.
Completes the object “something” in the giving-to-each example. Its indentation is restored from the native column alignment.

runs.text: Hum paßaro que tem duas cabe-

lines.note: Meimeichô is described as a bird with two heads. A visible line-end hyphen after cabe is restored, while the historical headword spelling is preserved.
Ças completes cabeças, adding that the bird has two beaks. The row is indented and closes the entry at the foot of column 1.
Meimǒ is paraphrased as midarini mayoo, wandering in error or confusion. Enlargement confirms three stems in the damaged m after Mei, despite loss of its second arch; the new headword is flush-left.
Completes the description of confusion caused by passions, ignorance, and similar causes. The historical spelling paixões and the unaccented ignorancia are preserved.
Meimon is an excellent saying or authoritative passage, paraphrased as suguretaru go. This independently printed headword is flush-left; ſentẽça retains the abbreviation mark.
Completes the authoritative-passage gloss and begins meimon wo asobasu. The example is ordinary Japanese text following a paragraph sign, not an embedded Portuguese term.

runs.text: Ler, ou dizer algũa boa ſentença.

lines.note: The example means reading or saying a good maxim or passage. The line closes the meimon entry.
Meimuco is a niece’s husband. This short kinship entry is flush-left, not a continuation of the saying or authority entry.
Meinichi is the day on which a person died, paraphrased as hito no shishitaru hi. The independent headword’s indentation is removed to match the scan.
Completes the death-day definition with “of someone.” Dalguem is retained as printed rather than modernized.
Meinin, paraphrased as mayoo hito, is a person who wanders in error. The headword is flush-left and the Portuguese erra-do is divided across rows.

runs.text: do, ou fora do caminho da ſaluação, &c.

lines.note: Do completes errado, followed by being outside the path of salvation. The religious framing belongs to the historical dictionary’s definition.
Meino mono is paraphrased as sugureta katana, an excellent Japanese sword. This is a new flush-left entry; catana is part of the Japanese synonym phrase, so it is not a typeface_terms candidate here.

runs.text: lente eſpada de Iapão feita por algum grande

lines.note: Completes excellente and specifies a sword from Japan made by a great craftsman. Iapão is Portuguese spelling and remains italic.
Official completes the maker’s description. The double f is visible and retained.
Meinu is a female dog. The final letter is u rather than provisional n, supported by the scan and the paired Portuguese Cadela; the headword is flush-left.
Meiqei is paraphrased as akirakana kagami and glossed as something clear and pure. The wording is retained literally instead of rewriting this gloss to match the later explicit mirror entry.
Completes “pure” and illustrates meiqeina hito, an upright person. This is an indented example under the preceding headword.
Candido completes the character description. The historical source associates clarity and purity with uprightness in the example.
Meiqen is becoming clear or something being distinctly revealed. Its flush-left position is restored; the divided cou- continues below.
Sa completes couſa, followed by claramente. This closes the disclosure sense before the homonymous sword entry.
The second meiqen is an excellent sword. Its separate flush-left entry is preserved rather than combined with the preceding disclosure sense.
Meiqet is paraphrased with akirakani isagiyoshi, clarity and purity. The clipped final t is the historical printed form.
Meiqet ni magire nashi states that there is no obscurity or ambiguity. The attached spelling maguirenaxi is retained as printed.

runs.text: Eſtà claro, & manifeſto, & não tem duuida.

lines.note: The Portuguese confirms clarity, manifestness, and absence of doubt. The grave accent in Eſtà and nasal mark in não are preserved.
Meiqiǒ and Meôqiǒ are the clear-mirror forms, paraphrased as akirakana kagami. The distinct circumflex and caron signs are retained occurrence by occurrence.
The Portuguese gives “clear mirror.” This short line completes the two alternative headword forms above.
Meiqiû is a cooing or singing dove, paraphrased as naku hato. The native scan has a circumflex over u, not the provisional caron; the following example independently uses the same û.
Completes the cooing or singing description and begins meiqiû ame wo yobu. Yo- continues the verb yobu on the next physical row.

runs.text: O gemer da rola adiuinha a chuua.

lines.note: Bu completes yobu; the Portuguese says the dove’s cooing foretells rain. This is the historical poetic example, with its final upright P. kept outside italics.
Meiqua denotes an excellent or beautiful rose in the Portuguese gloss. The source’s roſa is retained rather than generalized to a modern botanical category.
Meiquǒ is paraphrased as akirakana hikari and glossed as great radiance. The nasal abbreviations in Grãde and reſplãdor remain unexpanded.
The homonymous Meiquǒ means an excellent, upright, prudent king. The tilde in prudẽte is retained.
Mei reqireqi, equated with akirakana, describes something clear or manifest. The printed space after Mei is preserved, not silently collapsed into a modern compound.
Completes the clear-or-manifest explanation of mei reqireqi. The form appears openly or distinctly, as stated by manifeſtamente.

runs.text: Caminho eſcuro do inferno, ou por on-

lines.note: Meiro is a dark path to the underworld or the route taken by souls after death. The source’s wording is preserved without resolving it into a single doctrinal system.

runs.text: de vão as almas na outra vida.

lines.note: De completes onde, specifying where souls go in the other life. The nasal mark in vão is retained.

Meiſacu is an excellent or celebrated work. The damaged long-s sort is read with the clearer Meiſacuno on the next row and the work-of-craft gloss, correcting provisional Meifacu without importing modern spelling.
Meisaku no mono wa yoku hone wo kiru says that a masterwork cuts bone well. The scan closes this example with a comma, not the provisional period.

runs.text: A Catana que fez o inſigne official corta bem

lines.note: The Portuguese identifies the object as a sword made by an eminent craftsman. The missing i in inſigne is restored from the scan; Catana occurs inside Portuguese and is marked for whole-word typeface review.
Completes the statement that the sword cuts bones well. The printed oßos preserves the source’s double-s sort.
Meiſat is paraphrased as akirakani miru and glossed as seeing or passing judgment. The noun jui-zo is split across the physical line break.
Zo completes juizo, judgment upon something. The native crop includes the full descenders and the continuation remains indented.
Meisǒ, paraphrased as na no kusa, denotes an excellent herb. The short s and the final caron are retained, distinct from the later Meiſô entry.
A homonymous Meisǒ names a herb said to come from China. The source gives no further identification here, so none is supplied.
Meiſô is an eminent religious person. The scan has inſigne, restoring the omitted i; the headword uses long ſ and a circumflex, unlike the preceding herb forms.
Meiſui is paraphrased as na aru mizzu and glossed as excellent water. The doubled zz in mizzu and historical Portuguese Agoa are retained.

runs.text: Nome de hum peixinho do rio.

lines.note: Meitadaqi names a small river fish. The description is not expanded into a modern species identification unsupported by this row.
Meitaixǒ is paraphrased as na wo etaru taishoo, a renowned commander. The last word is Excellente rather than provisional Excellenta and continues as capitão below.

The scan reads lowercase italic capitão, completing the commander definition, not Napitão. The detached roman Meitet. at the far right is a catchword and has been moved to its own zone with a fresh ID.
Detached roman Meitet. at the lower right is page furniture rather than a new entry or part of capitão. Its full terminal t and period are retained.
